Mortgage renewal in four charts: the payment, the balance and the trade-off

See how a future renewal rate changes monthly cash flow, principal repayment and the relationship between rate and amortization.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hypothetical fixed-rate convention: quoted nominal annual rates compounded semi-annually, converted to equivalent monthly rates. Monthly payments at month-end. Actual contracts and compounding can differ; this is not an approval or a rate quote.

The central idea

A renewal changes the cost of financing the balance that remains. Test the payment against your budget while keeping the payoff date visible.

01

Separate the next contract from the payoff horizon

A mortgage term and its amortization answer different questions. The term describes the period covered by a particular contract. Amortization describes the repayment horizon used to calculate the scheduled payment. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s renewal guide explains these distinctions and the choices involved at renewal.

This illustration starts with a balance today, a current quoted rate and a remaining amortization. The assumed first term lasts five years. After 60 month-end payments, the renewal scenario applies a new rate to the balance still owed and recalculates the payment for the remaining years. The comparison keeps the original payoff date.

With the default CAD 400,000 balance, 20-year amortization and 4% quoted rate, the modeled monthly payment is CAD 2,416.99. A 6% renewal rate after five years changes it to CAD 2,750.51, an increase of CAD 333.53. These are original hypothetical calculations, not current lender offers or a forecast of rates.

02

Why two balance paths can reach zero together

The first chart compares continuing at the original rate with changing the rate after five years. Both balances reach the same scheduled end date because the renewal payment adjusts. A higher rate does not have to mean a longer loan when the payment increases enough to preserve amortization.

Do not read the balance line as the amount paid. A payment contains both interest and principal. Interest is a financing cost; principal reduces the debt. The stacked chart separates those components for years one through five and years six through ten in the renewal scenario.

Those two five-year periods start with different balances. Their interest amounts therefore reflect both the rate and the amount still owed. They are successive stages of one financing path, rather than two otherwise identical loans. For a rate-only comparison, use the matrix, which holds the initial balance constant across its cells.

03

Turn the payment change into a cash-flow test

The payment bars show the recurring budget effect more directly than the outstanding-balance lines. Compare the increase with the amount left after ordinary spending, other required debt payments and planned saving. A budget that balances only by suspending every other goal has little flexibility.

Try a higher renewal rate and record the monthly difference. Multiply that difference by twelve to estimate the annual cash-flow adjustment, while keeping it separate from a change in total interest over the full loan. The annual budget effect and lifetime borrowing cost answer different questions.

Property taxes, home insurance, condominium charges, repairs and utilities remain outside the payment calculation. A reserve for these costs can be necessary even when the mortgage payment itself fits. The emergency-fund guide provides a separate way to model an income interruption; mortgage affordability alone does not measure that resilience.

04

Read across the amortization matrix

Each cell shows the monthly payment for today’s selected starting balance, using the displayed rate and amortization. Reading across a row isolates the horizon change. Reading down a column isolates the rate change. The grid uses the starting balance, so its cells are not renewal quotes based on the smaller year-five balance.

At a positive rate, a longer amortization lowers the scheduled payment but keeps money borrowed for longer. Under an unchanged rate and a fully repaid loan, total scheduled interest is payment × number of payments − original principal. A lower monthly payment can therefore accompany a larger cumulative interest bill.

Actual renewal options may involve lender requirements, fees, insurance considerations, contractual restrictions or a reassessment of the application. The chart does not establish that a particular amortization is available. Obtain the actual terms before treating a modeled payment as an executable option.

05

Keep the compounding convention explicit

This example assumes a quoted nominal annual rate compounded semi-annually. If j is that annual rate as a decimal, the equivalent monthly rate is m = (1 + j ÷ 2)1/6 − 1. For balance B and N remaining monthly payments, the payment is Bm ÷ [1 − (1 + m)−N]. At zero interest, it is B ÷ N.

Each month’s interest is opening balance × m. The payment first covers that interest and the remainder reduces principal. At renewal, the formula uses the remaining balance and remaining number of payments. The selected renewal rate then stays constant until payoff in this model.

The tool excludes fees, prepayments, default-insurance premiums and later rate changes. Contracts can use different conventions. Read the lender’s disclosed interest calculation and payment schedule, then compare the resulting cash flows with this illustration. A useful review records the actual renewal date, balance, payment options and planned source of any increase.
